title: MCP 2026-07-28 Specification
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol steering group shipped the `2026-07-28` specification — described as the largest revision to MCP since its November 2024 launch. It delivers on the protocol's 2026 roadmap: making MCP viable for enterprise-scale production deployments rather than just local, single-user tool connections. See the [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents) page for MCP fundamentals; this page covers what changed in this revision.

---

## Stateless Protocol Core

Prior MCP versions assumed a long-lived, stateful connection between client and server (a natural fit for local stdio transports but awkward for HTTP-based deployments behind load balancers). The `2026-07-28` spec introduces a **stateless core**: servers no longer need to hold session state in memory tied to a single connection, so an MCP server can scale horizontally across ordinary HTTP infrastructure — the same load-balancer and autoscaling patterns used for any REST API.

---

## Multi Round-Trip Requests

A new request pattern lets a single logical operation span multiple HTTP round trips without requiring the client to maintain a persistent socket. This supports long-running tool calls and server-side elicitation (the server asking the client/user a follow-up question mid-call) without falling back to polling hacks.

---

## Header-Based Routing and Cacheable List Results

Routing metadata moved into HTTP headers rather than the request body, simplifying reverse-proxy and API-gateway configuration for MCP traffic. `tools/list`, `resources/list`, and similar list operations are now explicitly cacheable, reducing redundant round trips for clients (like Claude Code) that re-fetch a server's tool catalog frequently.

---

## Authorization Hardening and Enterprise-Managed Authorization

The spec tightens OAuth/OIDC alignment for MCP server authorization. Building on that, the **Enterprise-Managed Authorization** extension reached stable status in this cycle: organizations can centrally manage authorization for all their MCP servers, and end users authenticate once (single sign-on) to reach every connected server rather than authorizing each one individually. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are named adopters, alongside a growing set of third-party MCP servers.

---

## Formal Extensions Framework

Rather than growing the core spec indefinitely, `2026-07-28` formalizes an **extensions** mechanism — optional, versioned capabilities layered on the stateless core. Two notable extensions shipped alongside the core spec:

- **MCP Apps** — server-rendered UI components that a client can embed directly (e.g., a form or a visualization returned by a tool call, rendered natively instead of as raw text/JSON)
- **Tasks** — first-class support for long-running, asynchronous work: a tool call can return a task handle immediately and the client polls or is notified on completion, instead of holding a request open

---

## SDK and Adoption Status

Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript and Python) were updated for the new spec at launch. Combined download volume across both SDKs has crossed **1 billion total downloads**, with combined monthly downloads approaching **500 million**, reflecting MCP's growth from a niche Anthropic-authored standard into a widely adopted cross-vendor protocol.

---

## Why It Matters for Claude Code Users

Claude Code is an MCP client. Practically, this revision means:
- MCP servers you connect can be deployed as ordinary scalable HTTP services rather than single-process local servers
- Enterprise users can expect single-sign-on style access across all of an org's MCP servers, rather than authorizing each server separately
- Tool list caching should make session startup and tool-discovery faster when connecting to remote MCP servers
- Long-running tool calls (e.g., a build, a deploy, a large data job) can be modeled properly via the Tasks extension instead of blocking a connection open
